Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

You can never know who will harm you
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other endorsed items center on partner-violence-related threat monitoring, hypervigilance, sensory memory, and danger appraisals. In contrast, restrictive eating reflects a different coping theme that is not echoed elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and it sits awkwardly with the formulation in which Maladaptive Strategies feed Threat. Scanning surroundings and mirror checking plausibly amplify threat, but strict eating control does not connect clearly to the described trauma pattern.

vignette:
The assault happened in the kitchen of the apartment she had shared with her partner for three years. He had accused her of hiding money, and when she tried to walk away, he grabbed her by the hair, slammed her head against the counter, and then pressed a chef’s knife to her throat. Mai still remembers the cold flat of the blade against her skin, the way the metal glinted under the fluorescent light, and the sheer, silent terror that made her body go rigid. She did not scream; she did not move; she just waited until he released her, and then she fled. That moment, and the months of smaller cruelties before it, left something fractured inside her. She left the relationship, but the feeling of being permanently changed never faded. She came to believe that she was damaged now, that you could never know who would hurt you, and that she would always be an outsider, separate from people who had not been through what she had. These beliefs did not stay in her thoughts alone; they seeped into the very texture of her memories. Every time she recalled the knife, the terror flooded back as if it were happening again, but the events themselves felt disconnected—photographs she could see with horrifying clarity but that would not form a coherent story. The more she told herself she was forever changed, the more those memories came in jagged, unconnected pieces, each one carrying the same unbearable weight. And the memories themselves drove her deeper into that sense of being damaged: a loop that tightened with every flashback.

Now, nearly seven years later, Mai works as a private tutor, meeting students in their homes or at a local library. She is married to a kind man who knows little of the details, and she keeps her past carefully walled off. But the world feels saturated with threat. She notices potential weapons everywhere—scissors on a desk, a letter opener, even a heavy book with a sharp corner. Her body reacts before her mind registers the danger: her shoulders tighten, her breath catches, and she finds herself scanning the room for exits. This hypervigilance is relentless, and it feeds the memories. When she spots a lamp cord that could be used as a garrote, the image of the knife flashes in her mind, and she is back in that kitchen, her pulse hammering. To stop these images from overwhelming her, she started avoiding the kitchen altogether whenever she could, cooking only simple meals that required no knives. The threat she perceives is not abstract; it is concrete, immediate, and it drags the past into the present.

To manage this constant vigilance, Mai has developed strategies that she tells herself keep her safe. She habitually checks her surroundings, noting the position of every person, every object that could be used as a weapon. She catches herself checking mirrors—not for her own appearance, but to see who might be approaching from behind. She is especially watchful of men who match her ex-partner’s build or demeanor, and she will cross the street to avoid them. Unintentionally, these strategies have the opposite effect. The more she scans, the more she notices potential dangers; each opened drawer, each cleared room reveals another object that could become a weapon. Her own watchfulness generates new threats, and she never feels truly safe. This state of heightened awareness, in turn, strengthens the memories of the assault, because every sharp object or sudden movement is a reminder that she narrowly survived once and could be attacked again.

Her marriage has suffered. She avoids intimacy, certain that her husband would recoil if he knew what she had endured, and she often feels a deep loneliness even when he is beside her. In her tutoring sessions, she finds it hard to concentrate; she will stop mid-explanation to look at a pencil sharpener sitting on the table, her mind gone blank with fear. Recently, she had to cancel a session because the student’s father, a tall man with a deep voice, reminded her too much of her ex-partner, and she could not stop trembling. Her husband finally urged her to seek help after she woke him up screaming from a nightmare—another fragmented memory of the knife. Mai comes now because she is exhausted, because she cannot keep living this way, and because a small part of her still hopes that maybe, despite everything, she is not permanently broken.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that memories directly cause maladaptive strategies; instead, strategies are developed to manage threat, which is influenced by memories indirectly.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not show that memories directly cause maladaptive strategies; instead, strategies are developed to manage threat, which is influenced by memories indirectly.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
